newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. launches drive against female circumcision.
newsitem.headline: U.N. launches drive against female circumcision.

text.p: The heads of three United Nations agencies appealed on Wednesday for international support for a campaign to end the practice, widespread in Africa and parts of the Middle East, of female genital mutilation.

Launching the appeal at a news conference, World Health Organisation (WHO) Director-General Hiroshi Nakajima said some 130 million women and girls around the globe had been subjected to such mutilation and two million more were added each year.
"This practice is an infringement on the physical and psycho-integrity of women and is a form of violence against them," Nakajima declared.
The operation, sometimes called female circumcision, is common across Africa and involves usually very painful partial or total removal of external female genital organs, or their mutilation.

It is carried out, sociologists say, largely to encourage the woman -- whose enjoyment of sexual relations is seriously impaired -- to remain a virgin until marriage and so be more attractive to a potential husband.
Medical experts say it very often leads to death through infection, or at least life-long health problems, as well as infertility and complications in giving birth.
Nafis Sadik, Executive Director of the United Nations Population Fund, said many women and girls accepted the practice because they feared remaining unmarried.
"Women themselves appear to be a large part of the problem. We have to fight against the very people we are trying to protect," she said.
Carol Bellamy, Executive Director of the U.N. Children's Fund UNICEF, said although religious reasons were often given for the operation, "it only serves to keep women and girls 'in their place'."

She told the news conference the joint programme of the three agencies, which will provide teams to governments to help develop national policies, "provides the crucial momentum to once and for all eliminate" the practice.
Nakajima said campaigners "have to realise that female genital mutilation is a deeply-rooted practice....which can only be abolished completely when attitudes are changed."

According to the WHO, the age at which the operation is performed varies from region to region, being performed on infant girls just a few days old, on children and adolescents and even sometimes on mature women.
But in general, most girls undergo it between the ages of four and 12, the U.N. agency says.

In cultures where it is the accepted norm, it is normally performed by traditional practitioners with crude instruments from knives and razors to broken glass, usually without anaesthetics, according to the WHO.
In more affluent groups, it is sometimes performed in health clinics by qualified medical staff.

There has being growing concern in several West European countries -- and especially France -- over the spread of female circumcision in immigrant communities, where it is often performed by family grandmothers or practitioners brought in from Africa.

Bellamy and Sadik said there had been some progress in the fight against it, especially in Cameroon, Egypt and Uganda -- as well as in Burkina Faso, where the practice had been outlawed and practitioners face heavy fines and jail.
